entries.test: Whether prominent AGI-has-arrived claims (e.g., Chen et al. 2026 in Nature) rest mainly on benchmark and test performance, and whether historical AGI definitions put real-world flexibility at the centre.
entries.note: 'Confuse' is the authors' reading of others' reasoning. The checkable core is what those claims rely on and what the historical definitions said.

entries.test: Whether weaker redefinitions of AGI were put forward in recent years (e.g., economic or benchmark-based definitions), and whether any system has publicly shown the robustness and generalisation criteria of the original definitions.
entries.note: This is a co-authored essay in the 'we' voice. 'We see no evidence' reports the authors' own view, but the redefinition claim can be checked.
'A fundamental misunderstanding of how intelligence should be evaluated' is a judgment about how evaluation ought to work.

entries.test: Published evidence on whether benchmark contamination and training on benchmark-like synthetic data became more common in recent model development.
entries.note: Hard to measure directly, but studies of contamination exist.

entries.test: Whether the 2025 MIT NANDA 'State of AI in Business' report (and similar surveys) found that only a minority of firms report meaningful returns from AI deployment.
entries.note: The 'difficult to reconcile' part is interpretation. The checkable part is the survey finding.

entries.test: Whether Loru et al. (2025, PNAS) found that LLMs gave confident news-source reliability classifications where humans downgraded confidence, even when uncertainty was flagged in the input.
entries.note: Reports the co-authors' own published study.
A sweeping contrast between how humans and LLMs reason across whole domains, with no agreed test. The supporting citation is a conceptual preprint.

entries.test: Published evaluations of early-2026 frontier models for prompt-framing sensitivity, systematic failures and performance drops outside curated benchmarks.
entries.note: The measure is vague, but most readers would read it the same way.

entries.test: Whether frontier systems as of early 2026 showed robust, autonomous, goal-directed generalisation across novel environments (e.g., on novel-environment and long-horizon agent evaluations), without human scaffolding.
entries.note: Somewhat definitional, but the original AGI criteria give it a shared reading.
Calling the confusion a 'conceptual error' and a 'strategic misjudgment' is a judgment of worth.
